support.quote: In popular culture, Thompson and Dundy's killing of Topsy has switched attribution, with false claims that it was an anti-alternating current demonstration organized by Thomas Edison during the war of the currents.

support.quote: Born in Southeast Asia around 1875, Topsy was secretly brought into the United States soon thereafter and added to the herd of performing elephants at the Forepaugh Circus, who fraudulently advertised her as the first elephant born in the United States.

support.quote: In 1886, the Edison system was faced with new competition: an alternating current system initially introduced by George Westinghouse's company that used transformers to step down from a high voltage so AC could be used for indoor lighting.

support.quote: In May 1889 when New York had its first criminal sentenced to be executed in the electric chair, a street merchant named William Kemmler, there was a great deal of discussion in the editorial column of the New York Times as to what to call the then-new form of execution.

assessments.note: answer check: “William Kemmler” is on the snapshot of s2

support.quote: But was Edison to blame? Did he have anything to do with the execution of Topsy? The answer is an emphatic “no.”
Did Edison really electrocute Topsy the Elephant?
Captured on film by Thomas Edison, the event was one of a string of animal electrocutions Edison staged to discredit a new form of electricity: alternating current.

assessments.note: an example of the popular (wrong) attribution the question asks about; supports the answer 'Thomas Edison' as the inventor wrongly blamed
